abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Here we report on a Jehovah's Witness (JW) patient who experienced profound and prolonged life‐threatening cytopenias following CD19‐targeted CAR T cell therapy, successfully managed with bloodless medicine strategies. This case highlights the potential risks of CAR T therapy, even in patients without known hematotoxicity risk factors. By implementing tailored bloodless strategies, the patient received CAR T therapy without significant infectious, cardiac, or bleeding complications. Remarkably, they remain in remission 5 years later with normal blood counts. This underscores the viability of CAR T cell therapy for JW patients, emphasizing the importance of careful patient selection and risk‐benefit deliberation. Further research into severe cytopenias post‐CAR T therapy is critically needed.
Trial Registration: The authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.

sec.p: Keywords: cell therapy, cytopenia, Jehovah's witness, lymphomas

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: CD19‐targeting chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR T) therapy is an effective therapeutic option for relapsed/refractory B cell malignancies producing complete responses (CR) in 28%–68% of patients and long‐term durable response rates in the range of 30%–40% [1]. The most common adverse effects of CAR T cell therapy include the well‐described early toxicities of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicity. Hematologic toxicity is the less immediate life‐threatening complication but it is nearly universal, generally high grade, and frequently prolonged with many patients experiencing cytopenias beyond 1 month following CAR T infusion [2]. Hematologic toxicities are typically managed with growth factor support and blood product transfusions.

Individuals in the Jehovah's Witness (JW) community make faith‐based decisions to abstain from transfusions of whole blood and its primary components. This deeply personal decision presents unique considerations in the medical management of cytopenias. For individuals with hematologic malignancies, this means that while they actively seek life‐sustaining treatments, certain therapeutic options that typically involve blood transfusions may require careful discussion, adaptation, and identification of alternative management strategies. Successful bloodless medicine strategies using erythropoietin stimulating agents (ESAs), granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor (G‐CSF), thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO‐RAs), and blood conservation techniques have been widely used and reported on in the literature, making autologous and reduced intensity allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) viable options to those declining transfusion support [3, 4]. Here we report on a successful case of recovery from profound and prolonged pancytopenia after tisagenlecleucel (tisa‐cel) using aggressive bloodless management strategies in a JW patient.

sec.title: Case Presentation
sec.p: Our patient was a 68‐year‐old female at the time and she received CAR T cells in March 2020. She was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma in 2015. She was initially treated with six cycles of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R‐CHOP), achieving a metabolic CR. She went on to receive consolidation with (90)Y‐ibritumomab tiuxetan in March 2017. In August 2018, she was found to have progression of disease (POD) and started umbralisib in October 2018. In April 2019, she experienced POD again and idelalisib was initiated. In November 2019, imaging showed an enlarging cervical paraspinal mass. A biopsy revealed high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements. IgH gene rearrangement studies showed it to be clonally related to her underlying FL.

The patient and the medical team (inclusive of the patient's primary lymphoma physician and a cell therapy specialist) engaged in extensive discussions, which also included Hospital Liaison Committee members from her local congregation, to carefully consider treatment pathways. The subsequent risk‐benefit analysis for this patient was particularly complex, centering on balancing her deeply held conviction to abstain from blood transfusions with the aggressive biology of her double‐hit lymphoma. While technically feasible to perform a bloodless autologous HCT using meticulous blood conservation strategies and supportive measures, the outcomes for double‐hit lymphoma, even with full transfusion support, are generally poor. CAR T cell therapy offers high‐response rates and the potential for durable remissions in aggressive lymphomas, representing a more promising curative option. However, CAR T cell therapy itself carries substantial risks, including prolonged and severe cytopenias in addition to immune‐related toxicities such as CRS, which can be exacerbated by concomitant cytopenias (e.g., hypoxia worsened by anemia). Proceeding with CAR T cell therapy in the absence of blood transfusion support meant accepting these amplified risks and acknowledging the limited precedent and data for JW patients undergoing this intensive therapy [1, 2, 3, 4].

Following these extensive discussions, the patient opted for CAR T cell therapy. The choice between the specific constructs that were available at the time involved further risk‐benefit deliberation pertinent to the patient's unique situation. Tisa‐cel and axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi‐cel) were both commercially available at the time and are both effective products, but they appear to have different toxicity profiles despite the absence of head‐to‐head trials. Axi‐cel has been associated with higher incidence rates of CRS and ICANS, and potentially more rapid onset of these toxicities, compared to tisa‐cel. While both products can cause significant and prolonged cytopenias, tisa‐cel is also typically administered with lower doses of lymphodepleting chemotherapy. Given these differences, the patient underwent cell collection for tisa‐cel manufacturing in January 2020, followed by one cycle of rituximab, ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide (R‐ICE) as bridging therapy. Her CAR T infusion was delayed by 1 week due to significant anemia for which she received iron sucrose, vitamin B12, folic acid, and darbepoetin. Her white blood cell and platelet counts were within the normal range when she initiated lymphodepletion chemotherapy with fludarabine 25 mg/m2 and cyclophosphamide 250 mg/m2 × 3 doses followed by tisa‐cel infusion. CAR‐HEMATOTOX score was either 0 or 1 on a 0–7 scale (C‐reactive protein was not checked immediately prior to lymphodepletion), consistent with low risk for severe hematologic toxicity [5]. She was managed with aggressive bloodless strategies for JW as previously described [3]. She received daily supplementation of folic acid and vitamin B12, and weekly iron sucrose, darbepoetin, and oral vitamin K. Blood tests were minimized and microtainer collection tubes were used for blood draws. We did not use any early or preventive management strategies for CRS and ICANS given that only preliminary evidence was available at the time to support these strategies and their impact on cytopenias was unknown. We applied our standard antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral prophylaxis but avoided use of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole due to its potential hematologic toxicity. The patient's posttreatment course was complicated by Grade 1 CRS. She received G‐CSF for 2 days (Figure 1), and was discharged on Day +8. Following discharge, she continued folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation daily and received weekly iron sucrose.

caption.p: Outline of cytopenias and treatment administered. Range of doses of medications: G‐CSF (5–10 mcg/kg daily), iron sucrose (300–500 mg weekly), romiplostim (4–7 mcg/kg weekly), darbepoetin (100 mcg weekly), eltrombopag (50–150 mg daily), PO/IV aminocaproic acid (1–4 g every 4–6 h), IVIG (1 g/kg = 85 mg daily for 2 days), danazol (200 mg twice daily), methylprednisolone (90 mg twice daily then tapered off).

sec.p: She had an initial recovery of platelet and neutrophil counts to the normal range. On Day +22, she was found to have a petechial rash on the lower extremities with a platelet count of 27,000/µL, so romiplostim and oral aminocaproic acid were started. Subsequently, she continued to experience spontaneous ecchymoses on her lower extremities. On Day +36, she had a platelet count of 5000/µL and diffuse ecchymoses and was admitted to the hospital for closer surveillance and frequent dosing of intravenous aminocaproic acid. During her admission, she continued to be severely pancytopenic with a hemoglobin nadir of 4.4 g/dL and platelet count < 10,000/µL for 35 days (1000–2000/µL for 8 consecutive days). Extensive workup showed no evidence of infection, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, or immune‐mediated hemolysis. Inflammatory markers (Figure S1), LDH and liver function tests were not elevated. A bone marrow biopsy was deferred. She received escalating doses of G‐CSF, aminocaproic acid, romiplostim, darbepoetin, eltrombopag, and iron sucrose as depicted in Figure 1. Antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis was restarted given neutropenia. A course of methylprednisolone and several doses of IVIG were administered for a possible immune mechanism and danazol was administered due to its activity in other forms of bone marrow failure. She ultimately recovered her blood counts and was discharged after 37 days in the hospital. The patient remains in a durable complete remission nearly 5 years after tisa‐cel therapy, and her blood counts remain within the normal range.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The literature on the incidence, risk factors, and natural history of immune effector cell‐associated hematotoxicity (ICAHT) resulting from CD‐19‐directed CAR T cell therapy has grown in recent years. Cytopenias were the most common CTCAE grade ≥ 3 adverse event in the JULIET, ZUMA‐1, and TRANSCEND trials [1, 2, 3], and grade ≥ 3 cytopenias persisting beyond Day +30 following CAR T infusion occurred in up to a third of patients [6]. Real‐world evidence has further illustrated the high incidence of CAR T cell‐mediated hematotoxicity occurring both early (< 30 days) and late (> 90 days) post‐infusion, and commonly severe and prolonged [2, 5, 7, 8]. CAR T cells targeting BCMA have reported similar rates of prolonged cytopenias [9, 10].

Three distinct clinical phenotypes of hematologic recovery have been defined, primarily pertaining to neutrophil recovery: early, intermittent, and aplastic [2, 5, 7]. The early onset cytopenias are believed to occur due to the myelotoxic effects of chemotherapy, with or without a mechanism caused by the presence of CRS/HLH. On the other hand, the intermittent and aplastic phase of cytopenia is defined as that occurring well past chemotherapy or CAR‐associated cytopenia. The intermittent type is characterized as a biphasic or multiphasic recovery with subsequent decrease(s) in neutrophils after initial recovery. The aplastic type is severe, prolonged, and often refractory to growth factor support [11]. Our patient's pattern of myelosuppression was consistent with the intermittent type, which is associated with improved progression‐free and overall survival [11].

Given that infections are responsible for more than half of non‐relapse mortality cases after CAR T cell therapy [12], persistent and profound cytopenias are an important contributor to morbidity and mortality after CAR T [13, 14]. Consequences of anemia and thrombocytopenia are uncommon causes of death, however, in a patient who declines transfusion support, these risks are inflated and may place the patient in a prolonged life‐threatening situation.

Several risk factors that predispose to CAR T cell‐related cytopenias have been identified including the number of previous lines of therapy, prior HCT, older age, and high‐grade CRS. ICAHT is thought to be driven by the expansion of interferon‐γ producing cells in the bone marrow which suppress hematopoiesis [15]. Additional mechanisms that involve certain cytokines and chemokines have been proposed. A predictive model termed “CAR‐HEMATOTOX” was created to help identify the risk of hematological toxicity in CAR T therapy based on pre‐infusion baseline features [5]. This model assigns a score that indicates the likelihood of prolonged neutropenia, severe anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Interestingly, our patient's score determined before lymphodepletion was consistent with low risk. In addition to normal baseline marrow function, she experienced only low‐grade CRS, implying that additional risk factors are yet to be described.

Best practices for the management of persistent cytopenias have been published recently and are largely based on supportive care and investigating alternative etiologies that may cause cytopenias [2, 6]. Prospective data are lacking and the true impact of growth factor support and other interventions on the incidence of complications, non‐relapse mortality, and healthcare resource utilization should be examined.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: With the use of carefully adapted bloodless medicine strategies, our patient was able to receive CAR T cell therapy without having any significant infectious, cardiac, or bleeding events. Two other cases of successful bloodless CD19‐directed CAR T cell therapy were reported [16], although these patients did not develop profound cytopenias. While our patient's outcome was excellent, we urge significant caution in consideration of CAR T cell therapy as an option for those patients unable to receive blood and platelet transfusions. Patient selection and risk‐benefit deliberation are key, and it is preferable to have a shared decision‐making model that includes a cell therapy specialist and a disease‐specific oncologist as well as experts in psychosocial aspects of cancer care (i.e., a social worker and a liaison psychiatrist or psychologist). A critical initial step involved a thorough exploration of the patient's individual preferences regarding various blood products, as the acceptance of minor blood fractions can vary among JWs based on personal conscience. This nuanced understanding formed the foundation for evaluating options such as “bloodless” autologous HCT or CAR T cell therapy. Hospital Liaison Committee members are individuals who formally liaise with the medical community on behalf of JW patients, particularly regarding bloodless medicine and surgery. These members do not make medical decisions but rather act as a communication bridge between patients, family members, and medical teams, to ensure clear understanding and respect for the patient's advance medical directives, and alignment between treatment planning and a patient's beliefs. In sum, the approach must be highly individualized, balancing clinical aggressiveness of disease with treatment feasibility, supportive care infrastructure (including social workers and psychologists), and patient autonomy. Further understanding of the mechanisms and risk factors for severe cytopenias as well as their proper management, is also critically needed.
